newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen exporting zinc ore on high world prices.
newsitem.headline: China seen exporting zinc ore on high world prices.

text.p: Chinese zinc mines are exporting their ore to take advantage of high prices and to avoid the cashflow problems of domestic smelters, traders said on Wednesday.

Traders' estimates of exports so far this year range from 30,000-40,000 tonnes to 80,000-90,000 tonnes, and while the divergence is wide, any exports are seen further squeezing an already-tight market.
"This year is going to be the best year for Chinese zinc concentrate exports, everyone is selling on the overseas market," a trader in Beijing said.
Chinese customs figures were not available. One industry source, however, said China exported 57,000 tonnes of zinc concentrate in the final quarter of 1996.
The Beijing source said trading houses were now buying concentrate from Chinese mines to sell to Asia and Europe.
Some Chinese smelters are already short of raw material because they have no cash to pay for supplies, traders said.

A producer source in the region said China's smelters had for a long time done tolling deals -- in which trading houses provide smelters with concentrate they process into metal and return for a fee -- to overcome their cashflow problems.
"There have always been cashflow problems with the smelters so it would make sense for the mines to export if they can get paid," the producer source said.
"It has been a long time between drinks for the mines, and they don't want to miss out on the good times," he said, referring to the recent rally in world zinc prices.
Zinc prices on the London Metal Exchange have risen considerably in the past four months, hitting a 4-1/2 year high on March 17 of more than $1,300 a tonne.
Prices have barely changed this week, ending on Tuesday down $3 at $1,264, after trading between $1,272 and $1,261, as the trade waits to see how much metal will move out of China.

China's growing demand for refined zinc has seen the country transformed since 1994 from a net concentrate exporter to a net importer. Net exports in 1994 were 87,000 tonnes of contained zinc in concentrates. Last year China's net imports were 92,800 tonnes, according to the industry source.
Stocks are believed to have run dry at most Chinese smelters, with few exceptions.
Zhuzhou, considered to be one of China's few reputable and liquid zinc makers, is having no problem sourcing ore, traders said.

A marketing source at the smelter recently told Reuters that Zhuzhou had 40,000 tonnes of zinc concentrate on hand which he said was one to two months' supply. One tonne of zinc metal usually requires two tonnes of concentrate.
The trade generally agrees world zinc metal supply is heading for a deficit of more than 200,000 tonnes in the second half of 1997 which could see prices move higher, possibly to $1,400.
The rally in metal prices spills over to concentrate, and the higher the metal price the greater the return to the mines.
Chinese concentrate for export is being loaded at major ports FOB (free on board) at a discount of $150-200 based on a metal price of $1,000 a tonne, a Hong Kong source said.
Concentrate in China is fetching about 4,400 yuan ($530) a tonne, a Chinese trader said.
Between 22,000 and 30,000 tonnes a month of Chinese zinc metal is being exported, most to LME warehouses in Singapore where it is mainly used as collateral for loans, sources say.
Most of that is currently coming from Zhuzhou -- 15,000 to 20,000 tonnes over the past couple of months -- which has said it hopes to produce 210,000 tonnes of metal this year and export half of it.
Traders said they expected Chinese zinc metal exports to hit 350,000-400,000 tonnes this year, up from the annual average of 300,000 tonnes, to take advantage of strong values.
-- Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-8544
